title: Nextflow basic
text:
Understanding Nextflow Processes and Channels
For more detailed training, the official Nextflow training is available here: training.nextflow.io.

Process blocks
In Nextflow, a process represents one step of a pipeline. It can run a command, a script, or a bioinformatics tool.
A process generally contains four main parts:
process PROCESS_NAME {

    // directives
    container 'my_container'

    input:
    data z
    data y
    data x

    output:
    path x
    path y
    path z

    script:
    task1
    task2
    task3

}

input: defines the data that the process needs.
Directives specify how the process should be executed, for example which container, CPU, memory, or execution environment to use.
script: contains the commands that will actually be executed.
output: defines the files or data produced by the process.

The important idea is that a process focuses on one specific task, while Nextflow takes care of connecting the different processes together.


Channels
Channels are used to transfer data between processes.
For example, the output of one process can be sent through a channel and become the input of another process:
Process A
    │
    ▼
 Channel
    │
    ▼
Process B
This allows the different steps of a pipeline to communicate without having to manually manage the transfer of files between them.
Nextflow has two main types of channels:


1. Queue channels
A queue channel behaves like a queue of data.
Each item is consumed when a process reads it. Once an item has been consumed, it cannot normally be read again from the same queue channel.
For example, imagine a channel containing three samples:
Channel
 ├── sample1
 ├── sample2
 └── sample3
A process can consume these samples one by one:
sample1 → Process
sample2 → Process
sample3 → Process
This is particularly useful when processing many samples in a workflow.
Queue channels are therefore useful when data should flow through the pipeline and be consumed by downstream processes.


2. Value channels
A value channel contains a single value that can be read multiple times without being consumed.
For example:
Value channel
      │
      ├──→ Process A
      ├──→ Process B
      └──→ Process C
All three processes can access the same value.
This is useful when the same information needs to be reused by several processes, such as a reference genome, a parameter, or a configuration value.


Queue vs Value channels
The main difference is therefore how the data is consumed:








Channel type
Content
Can be read multiple times?




Queue channel
A stream/queue of values
❌ Normally consumed once


Value channel
A single value
✅ Yes, unlimited times



Understanding the difference is important when designing more complex Nextflow workflows, especially when the same data needs to be used by several processes.
For more details, see the official Nextflow documentation on channel types.
Execution Abstraction Process → defines what should be executed.
Executor → defines where and how it is executed (local, HPC, cloud).
This separation makes Nextflow workflows portable across different computing environments.
Nextflow uses a Groovy-based DSL, but processes can run scripts written in Bash, Python, R, Perl, Ruby, etc.
First Nextflow script — l’essentiel


Setup the environment
screen -S nextflow
pixi init -c bioconda -c conda-forge
pixi add nextflow 


hello.nf structure

params → input parameters
process → processing steps
input / output → data entering/leaving a process
script → commands to execute
workflow → connects processes and channels
Channel.of() → creates a channel
.flatten() → splits elements for individual processing
.view() → displays channel contents

Key idea: Processes do the work, channels transport data, and workflows connect the steps.


Run
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf


Output

executor > local → runs locally
SPLITLETTERS (1) → 1 task
CONVERTTOUPPER (2) → 2 tasks, potentially in parallel
96/fd5f07 → task ID / directory in work/
HELLO, WORLD! → final output

Important: Parallel tasks do not guarantee output order.


-resume
Nextflow caches process results and re-runs only the processes that changed.
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume
Key point: unchanged processes are skipped and their cached results are reused.


Workflow parameters
Define parameters with params.name and override them from the command line with --name:
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume --greeting 'Bonjour le monde!'


Configuration priority
From highest to lowest priority:

Command-line parameters
-params-file
-c configuration file
nextflow.config in current directory
Project nextflow.config
$HOME/.nextflow/config
Parameters defined in the script



Clean up
View previous runs:
pixi run nextflow log
Clean the cache and work/ directories:
pixi run nextflow clean -f
Specify the run name and option as explained Here.
Clean runs before a specific run:
pixi run nextflow clean -before <RUN_NAME> -f
Key point: Nextflow stores cached results in work/; clean it periodically when the cache is no longer needed.

title: Nextflow basic
text:
Simple RNA-seq pipeline:
Reads ──► FASTQC ───────────────┐
                               ├──► MULTIQC
Reads ──► QUANTIFICATION ──────┘
                ▲
                │
Transcriptome ─► INDEX



Salmon → transcript quantification
FastQC → read quality control
MultiQC → final QC report


Key point: FASTQC and QUANTIFICATION are independent and can run in parallel.






nextflow.config:
process {
    executor = "slurm"
    time = '2.h'
    cpus = 4
}

resume = true
singularity.enabled = true

executor {
    account = 'your_project_account'
}





Parameter
Purpose




executor = "slurm"
Run processes on the cluster


time
Maximum task runtime


cpus
Number of CPUs


resume = true
Reuse cached results


singularity.enabled = true
Enable containers


account
SLURM project/account








params.reads = "$projectDir/data/ggal/gut_{1,2}.fq"
params.transcriptome_file = "$projectDir/data/ggal/transcriptome.fa"
params.multiqc = "$projectDir/multiqc"
params.outdir = "results"


The main project directory.
project/
├── data/
├── results/
└── script.nf

container
container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7'
The container specifies the software environment used to run the process.
Here, the container provides:
Software : Salmon
Version  : 2.7.0
Source   : Seqera Wave
It avoids installing Salmon directly on the cluster and helps ensure a reproducible environment.
With:
singularity.enabled = true
Nextflow can run the container using Singularity/Apptainer.

Key point: container = which software environment should run the process?

title: Introduction to Pixi
text: Pixi is a fast, modern, and reproducible package management tool for developers of all backgrounds.

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Adding Software to the Environment
Adding a dependency to the project tells Pixi to install that software.
Use:
pixi add <package>
For example:
pixi add quarto
You should run pixi add from inside the Pixi project directory.

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Running Software with Pixi
Once a tool has been installed in the Pixi environment, you can run it using:
pixi run quarto --help
This works even if quarto is not installed globally on your system.
In contrast:
quarto --help
may not work because Quarto is installed only inside the Pixi environment.

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Entering the Environment
Alternatively, you can enter the environment with:
pixi shell
Once inside the environment, you can use the installed tools directly:
quarto --help
This is somewhat similar to activating a Conda environment.
To leave the environment:
exit

Note: pixi shell may not be available or may behave differently on some HPC systems. For example, it does not work as expected on HPC2N. In such cases, pixi run can be used instead.

title: Quality Control
text: Quality control of sequencing data screen, slurm, pixi, FastQC, MultiQC

title: Quality Control
text:
Quality Control of Sequencing Data
Quality control (QC) is essential before downstream analysis because poor-quality sequencing data can affect the reliability of the results. FastQC is used to assess the quality of raw sequencing reads, while MultiQC summarizes results from multiple samples.

🔬 Main concepts

FASTQ → common format for raw sequencing reads; each read contains the sequence and its quality scores.
FastQC → checks sequencing quality and provides an HTML report with different QC metrics.
Pixi → creates a reproducible environment and installs FastQC.
SLURM → manages computational resources and jobs on the HPC cluster.
srun → runs a command interactively on allocated HPC resources.
sbatch → submits a script as a batch job, which is useful for running analyses on multiple samples or repeating them later.
MultiQC → combines QC results from multiple FastQC reports into a single summary report.



🧪 Typical QC workflow
Raw FASTQ
    ↓
FastQC
    ↓
Individual QC reports
    ↓
MultiQC
    ↓
Combined QC report
    ↓
Assess data quality


Screen / GNU Screen
Screen (GNU Screen) is a terminal multiplexer. It allows you to start a persistent terminal session and run processes inside it. Processes continue running even when the session is detached or the connection is interrupted.

Start a named session
screen -S fastqc


Detach from the session
Press:
Ctrl + a, then d
The processes inside the session will continue running.


List running Screen sessions
screen -ls


Reattach to a session
screen -r fastqc



Creating Symbolic Links
The command below creates symbolic links to the original FASTQ files: ln -s path/to/common_data/wgs/*fastq.gz .


Why use symbolic links?
Avoid duplicating large sequencing files. Keep the original raw data unchanged. Make files easily accessible from your analysis directory. Save storage space.


💻 Example
Run FastQC on HPC:
srun -A project_ID -t 15:00 -n 1 \
  pixi run fastqc --noextract -o fastqc data/*fastq.gz
For a reproducible batch analysis:
sbatch fastqc.sh


🔑 Key takeaway
Pixi manages the software environment → SLURM manages HPC resources → FastQC checks individual sequencing files → MultiQC summarizes the results.
Before proceeding with downstream analysis, always inspect the QC results and determine whether the data quality is suitable for the planned analysis.

title: nf-core
text:
nf-core is a community-driven collection of open-source Nextflow pipelines for bioinformatics. It also provides reusable modules, training materials, documentation standards, and development templates.



🧬 Ready-to-use pipelines for many bioinformatics analyses
🔄 Reproducible and portable through Nextflow and containers
📚 Extensive and standardized documentation
📦 Reusable modules and standardized workflows
⚙️ Input validation and standardized configuration
🔁 Supports Nextflow features such as parallel execution and resume


Important: nf-core pipelines should not be treated as black boxes. You are still responsible for checking whether the pipeline, input data quality, parameters, and outputs are appropriate for your analysis.




The nf-core website provides a catalog of available pipelines.
For each pipeline, check:

Usage → how to run it and required inputs
Parameters → available options
Output → files and results produced

For example, nf-core/rnaseq is a pipeline for RNA-seq analysis.



For HPC systems using SLURM, a configuration file defines how Nextflow should submit jobs and which resources are available.
Important settings include:

max_memory
max_cpus
max_time
executor = 'slurm'

For example, an HPC2N configuration can be downloaded with:
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hpc2n/intro-course/master/exercises/NEXTFLOW/INTERACTIVE/hpc2n.config
The compute project must then be specified in the configuration.



Example using nf-core/rnaseq, a variant-calling pipeline:
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
  -profile test \
  --outdir rnaseq_test \
  -c hpc2n.config
Key options:

pixi run → use the Pixi environment
nextflow run → execute a Nextflow pipeline
nf-core/sarek → pipeline to run
-profile test → use the built-in test data/profile
--outdir → output directory
-c → HPC configuration file




After running a pipeline, always check:
What happened? → What outputs were generated? → Are the results and pipeline appropriate for my data?

title: nf-core
text:
Configure the Pipeline
The nf-core launcher helps generate the parameters required to run the pipeline.
For nf-core/rnaseq, the main files to prepare are:

Samplesheet (.csv) → describes the samples and FASTQ files.
Reference genome (.fa) → the reference genome used for the analysis.
GTF file (.gtf) → provides the gene/transcript annotations.
Parameter file (nf-params.json) → contains the configuration of the run.
HPC configuration (hpc2n.config) → defines how Nextflow runs on the HPC cluster.

Use absolute paths for files and directories, especially when working on an HPC system.

1. Create the samplesheet
Create a CSV file, for example:
Samplesheet.csv
The samplesheet contains the following columns:
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness,seq_platform
Example:
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness,seq_platform
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L002_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L002_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto,ILLUMINA
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L003_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L003_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto,ILLUMINA
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L004_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L004_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto,ILLUMINA

sample → sample identifier
fastq_1 → forward/read 1 FASTQ file
fastq_2 → reverse/read 2 FASTQ file
strandedness → library strandedness (auto in this example)
seq_platform → sequencing platform (ILLUMINA here)

The FASTQ filenames should correspond to the files available in your data/ directory.


2. Add the reference files
For the RNA-seq analysis, provide:

the reference genome in FASTA format (.fa or .fa.gz)
the corresponding GTF annotation (.gtf or .gtf.gz)

For example:
Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna_sm.primary_assembly.fa.gz
Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.108.gtf.gz
These files should be accessible from the HPC and their absolute paths should be specified in the parameter file.


3. Create the parameter file
Create a file named:
nf-params.json
Example:
{
    "input": "/proj/nobackup/repbio26/ndeye/nf-core-rnaseq/Samplesheet.csv",
    "outdir": "/proj/nobackup/repbio26/ndeye/nf-core-rnaseq/",
    "fasta": "/proj/nobackup/repbio26/ndeye/nf-core-rnaseq/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna_sm.primary_assembly.fa.gz",
    "gtf": "/proj/nobackup/repbio26/ndeye/nf-core-rnaseq/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.108.gtf.gz",
    "save_reference": true
}
The main parameters are:

input → path to the samplesheet
outdir → directory where results will be saved
fasta → path to the reference genome
gtf → path to the GTF annotation
save_reference → must be added manually to the JSON file after using the nf-core launcher. Setting it to true tells the pipeline to save the reference files generated/prepared during the run for future reuse.



4. Run the pipeline on HPC
Use the HPC configuration file to specify the SLURM executor and available resources.
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
  -r 3.26.0 \
  -resume \
  -params-file nf-params.json \
  -c hpc2n.config
The main components are:

pixi run → use the Pixi environment
nextflow run → run Nextflow
nf-core/rnaseq → RNA-seq pipeline
-r 3.26.0 → pipeline version
-resume → reuse successfully completed processes
-params-file nf-params.json → use the pipeline parameters
-c hpc2n.config → use the HPC/SLURM configuration

The pipeline can also be submitted through SLURM using sbatch.


5. Monitor
Check running jobs:
squeue -u your_username


Useful links

nf-core
nf-core pipelines
nf-core/rnaseq
nf-core/Sarek
nf-core documentation
Nextflow training
Custom reference genomes

title: Containers
text:
Containers make bioinformatics analyses more reproducible by packaging software together with its dependencies and environment.
They help avoid problems caused by:

Different operating systems or software versions
Conflicting dependencies
Outdated bioinformatics tools
Needing different versions of the same software

A container image is portable and immutable, making it easier to run the same software environment on different systems.



Several tools can be used to run containers, including Docker, Apptainer, and Podman.
For HPC and multi-user servers, we commonly use Apptainer.



Container images can be downloaded from registries such as Docker Hub or Seqera/Wave.
For example, from Docker Hub:
apptainer pull vcftools.sif docker://biocontainers/vcftools:v0.1.16-1-deb_cv1
From Seqera:
apptainer pull vcftools.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/vcftools:0.1.17--b541aa8d9f9213f9
The .sif file is the local Apptainer container image.





apptainer exec runs a specific command inside the container:
apptainer exec vcftools.sif vcftools --version
This is particularly useful in bioinformatics because we usually want to run a specific tool inside the container.



apptainer run executes the container’s predefined %runscript:
apptainer run container.sif



apptainer shell opens an interactive shell inside the container:
apptainer shell container.sif
You can then use the tools installed inside the container.




By default, not all directories from the host system are accessible inside a container.
The -B option allows you to bind a directory from the host into the container:
apptainer exec -B ../data:/rawdata container.sif ls /rawdata
Here, the host directory ../data is accessible inside the container as /rawdata.



Apptainer can be used directly inside a SLURM batch job:
#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A project_ID
#SBATCH -t 30:00
#SBATCH -n 1

apptainer exec container_image.sif \
    fastqc -o . --noextract ../data/*fastq.gz
This combines SLURM resource management with a reproducible software environment.



If a suitable container image does not already exist, you can build your own using a .def definition file.
The main sections are:

Bootstrap / From → choose the base image
%post → install software and dependencies
%environment → configure environment variables
%runscript → define the default action of the container

For example:
Bootstrap: docker
From: ubuntu:22.04

%post
    apt-get -y update
    apt-get -y install cowsay

%environment
    export LC_ALL=C

%runscript
    date | cowsay
Build the container with:
apptainer build mycontainer.sif mycontainer.def
Then run it with:
apptainer run mycontainer.sif






Command
Purpose




apptainer run
Executes the container’s %runscript


apptainer exec
Runs a specific command inside the container


apptainer shell
Opens an interactive shell inside the container



In bioinformatics workflows, exec is often the most useful command because it allows us to explicitly run a particular tool and version inside the container.
